citeAs: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt (2021). Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset. NeurIPS 2021 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks.
creator: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt (UC Berkeley / UChicago)
description: MATH is a dataset of 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems (7,500 training and 5,000 test) drawn from high school math competitions including the AMC 10, AMC 12, and AIME. Each problem includes a full step-by-step solution written in LaTeX and natural language, and problems are tagged by difficulty level (1–5) and span seven subjects including Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting and Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, and Precalculus.
name: MATH
rai:annotationsPerItem: Each problem has one step-by-step solution and one final boxed answer.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Problems and solutions were sourced from mathematics competitions (AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME) and curated by the competition mathematics community. Difficulty levels (1–5) follow AoPS conventions: a subject's easiest problems are assigned level 1 and hardest problems level 5. Final answers are formatted to follow consistent rules enabling exact-match evaluation.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset focuses on competition mathematics from the United States (AMC, AIME), which assesses the mathematical problem-solving ability of the best young mathematical talent in the United States. Problems span seven subjects but are limited to competition-style problems rather than broader mathematical domains.
rai:dataCollection: Problems were collected from high school mathematics competitions including the AMC 10, AMC 12, and AIME, many of which are available from aops.com. These competitions span decades and assess the mathematical problem-solving ability of the best young mathematical talent in the United States.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Competition mathematics problems from the AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and other contests, sourced from aops.com. Problems are created by the Mathematical Association of America (MAA) and span decades of competition history.
rai:dataLimitations: Large language models achieve only 3.0%–6.9% accuracy on MATH, indicating it is extremely challenging. Assuming a log-linear scaling trend, models would need around 10^35 parameters to achieve 40% accuracy, making pure scaling impractical. The dataset requires new algorithmic advancements rather than just scale to achieve strong performance.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems and solutions are consistently formatted using LaTeX and the Asymptote vector graphics language. Final boxed answers follow consistent formatting rules: probabilities as simplified fractions, matrix entry fractions encoded with x/y, other fractions with \frac{x}{y}, coefficients without multiplication symbols, expressions with multiple variables in alphabetical order, and polynomials in decreasing degree order.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to advance mathematical reasoning in AI. However, even 40% accuracy for a machine learning model would have ramifications for cheating on homework. The authors explicitly state they do not intend for the dataset to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking mathematical problem-solving ability of machine learning models; training models to generate step-by-step answer derivations and explanations; measuring and forecasting reasoning capabilities of AI systems. The dataset is not intended to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams.

evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems and solutions are consistently formatted using LATEX and the Asymptote vector graphics language. To assess models using exact match, we force the ﬁnal boxed answers to follow consistent formatting rules. Speciﬁcally, probabilities are expressed as simpliﬁed fractions. Moreover, matrix entry fractions are encoded with x/y, while all other fractions are consistently encoded with the \frac{x}{y} command.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: Dataset Intended Uses. We document the dataset within the paper and note that the dataset and code for reproducing results is available at https://github.com/hendrycks/apps. We do not intend for this dataset to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams. We intend for others to use this dataset in order to better forecast reasoning capabilities.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: Accuracy also increases only modestly with model size: assuming a log-linear scaling trend, models would need around 1035 parameters to achieve 40% accuracy on MATH, which is impractical. Instead, to make large strides on the MATH dataset with a practical amount of resources, we will need new algorithmic advancements from the broader research community.

evidence.rai:annotationsPerItem: Each problem has a step-by-step solution and a ﬁnal boxed answer. Example problems with step-by-step solutions are shown in Figure 1.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: We encode a problem's difﬁculty level from '1' to '5,' following AoPS. A subject's easiest problems for humans are assigned a difﬁculty level of '1,' and a subject's hardest problems are assigned a difﬁculty level of '5.' Concretely, the ﬁrst few problems of an AMC 8 exam are often level 1, while AIME problems are level 5.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: These competitions span decades and assess the mathematical problem-solving ability of the best young mathematical talent in the United States. Unlike most prior work, most problems in MATH cannot be solved with a straightforward application of standard K-12 mathematics tools.
